title: Methylene Chloride; Regulation Under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA); Compliance Date Extension
summary:
The EPA just gave non‑federal laboratories an extra 18 months to meet new workplace safety requirements for using methylene chloride, aligning their deadlines with federal labs. Separately, the FAA made a routine update to an instrument approach at the Sioux Falls, SD airport.

For labs, this means more time to roll out monitoring, exposure controls, and safety plans without interrupting critical work. Universities, commercial testing firms, environmental labs, wastewater facilities, and law enforcement labs stand to benefit. These groups often rely on methylene chloride to run required methods for things like water, soil, and air testing, and many said they couldn’t realistically switch solvents or hire specialists fast enough to meet the earlier dates. The EPA’s goal is to prevent disruptions to public health and safety services while labs put stronger protections in place.

Here are the new milestones in plain terms: initial air monitoring by November 9, 2026; set up controlled work areas and meet exposure limits by February 8, 2027; and have full exposure control plans and methods in place by May 10, 2027. The rule takes effect December 15, 2025. The EPA says the change doesn’t add new requirements—it delays when they start—so near‑term costs are lower, though the health benefits of tighter protections will also start later.

Who could be negatively affected? Workers and nearby communities may wait longer for the added protections the original rule promised, which is why some commenters opposed any delay. There’s also a fairness question for organizations that already invested to meet the earlier dates. On the other hand, labs argue that rushing would have forced them to pause or drop essential testing, creating its own risks to public health and environmental oversight.

In short, the EPA is trying to balance safety with practicality: keep vital testing running while giving labs time to implement stronger protections. The FAA’s change is a standard procedural update affecting one airport and doesn’t carry broader policy impacts.
